challenges.title: Mean vs Median With Outlier
challenges.prompt: Which statistic best represents a typical order value?
options: Median, because the extreme ₹7,500 order pulls the mean upward
Mean, because it always describes the middle customer
Mode, because every dataset must have one
challenges.expectedAnswer: Median, because the extreme ₹7,500 order pulls the mean upward
challenges.insightPrompt: Write a short insight explaining the outlier effect and what metric you would report.
hints: Compare mean sensitivity to extreme values.
The median uses rank, not magnitude.
A typical-value metric should resist one extreme order.
challenges.explanation: Median is more robust than mean when a small sample contains a large outlier.

challenges.title: Recognize Right-Skewed Delivery Time
challenges.context: Most deliveries take 20–30 hours, but a few disruption cases take 80–100 hours.
options: Right-skewed distribution
Perfectly symmetric normal distribution
Uniform distribution
challenges.insightPrompt: Explain what the long tail means for how you summarize delivery time.
hints: The rare values are much larger than the typical values.
A long high-value tail is right skew.
Consider percentiles as well as averages.
challenges.explanation: A few very long delays create a right tail and can distort the mean.

challenges.title: Correlation Without Causal Overclaim
challenges.context: Accounts with more training sessions show higher retention, but larger customers also buy more training.
options: Training attendance is associated with retention, but account size and other factors may confound the relationship
Training sessions definitely cause all retention improvement
The relationship should be ignored because correlation is useless
challenges.expectedAnswer: Training attendance is associated with retention, but account size and other factors may confound the relationship
challenges.insightPrompt: Write the finding and one next analysis that would reduce causal uncertainty.
hints: Association is useful but not automatically causal.
Large accounts may differ in many ways.
Suggest a controlled or segmented next step.
challenges.explanation: Confounding variables can explain part of an observed correlation.

challenges.title: Interpret an A/B Test
challenges.context: Variant B converts at 5.4% versus 5.0% for A, but p=0.18 and the confidence interval includes zero lift.
options: The result is inconclusive; the observed lift is not strong enough to rule out sampling noise
Variant B is proven better because 5.4% is larger
Variant A is proven better because p is above 0.05
challenges.expectedAnswer: The result is inconclusive; the observed lift is not strong enough to rule out sampling noise
challenges.insightPrompt: Summarize the evidence and recommend what to do next.
hints: Observed difference is not the same as statistical evidence.
The interval still allows no lift.
Recommend more evidence rather than declaring a winner.
challenges.explanation: An inconclusive test should not be converted into a confident winner/loser claim.

challenges.title: Control False Positive Risk
challenges.context: A team tests 40 customer segments independently and highlights every p<0.05 result.
options: False positives from multiple testing
Only false negatives
No statistical risk because 0.05 is always safe
challenges.insightPrompt: Explain the risk and name a safer analysis practice.
hints: More tests create more chances for chance significance.
Think family-wise error or false discovery.
Use correction or validation.
challenges.explanation: Multiple comparisons inflate the chance of false positive findings unless controlled.

challenges.title: Diagnose an Underpowered Experiment
challenges.context: A retention experiment has only 80 accounts per arm and the minimum meaningful lift is small.
options: The test may be underpowered to detect the meaningful lift reliably
Small samples always prove no effect
Power does not depend on sample size
challenges.expectedAnswer: The test may be underpowered to detect the meaningful lift reliably
challenges.insightPrompt: State the limitation and what you would calculate before the next test.
hints: Power depends partly on sample size.
Small effects require more information.
Plan the next sample from the minimum detectable effect.
challenges.explanation: Power analysis links sample size to the effect size the business cares about detecting.

challenges.title: Hypothesis Test for Wait Time
challenges.context: Average wait time rose from 48 to 54 minutes after a scheduling change, with high day-to-day variation.
challenges.prompt: What is the best next step?
options: Test the change with an appropriate comparison and confidence interval while checking day mix and capacity conditions
Assume the six-minute increase was caused by scheduling
Ignore variability because averages are enough
challenges.expectedAnswer: Test the change with an appropriate comparison and confidence interval while checking day mix and capacity conditions
challenges.insightPrompt: Write a cautious operational interpretation and next step.
hints: The average changed, but variability matters.
Check whether operating mix changed too.
Use uncertainty around the difference.
challenges.explanation: A hypothesis test is useful only alongside assumptions, context and effect-size interpretation.

challenges.title: Separate Seasonality From Trend
challenges.context: Shipments rise every Friday and Saturday but stay flat across months after adjusting for weekday.
options: Day-of-week seasonality without a clear monthly trend
Strong monthly growth trend
Pure random noise with no repeatable pattern
challenges.expectedAnswer: Day-of-week seasonality without a clear monthly trend
challenges.insightPrompt: Explain how this should influence a throughput forecast.
hints: The pattern repeats by weekday.
After adjustment, months are flat.
Forecasts should model the repeatable calendar effect.
challenges.explanation: Seasonality is a repeatable calendar pattern and should be modeled separately from trend.

challenges.title: Executive Revenue Trend
challenges.context: The CEO wants monthly revenue direction and whether order volume explains the change.
challenges.prompt: Choose the visual and KPI set.
challenges.insightPrompt: Write the executive insight you would put below the chart.
hints: Time is ordered.
Separate volume from value per order.
Avoid unrelated HR metrics.
challenges.explanation: A line chart preserves time order; revenue, orders and AOV explain whether growth comes from volume or basket size.

challenges.title: Compare Product Categories
challenges.context: Merchandising wants to compare revenue and margin across six product categories.
challenges.prompt: Choose the chart and KPI set.
chartOptions: Line chart treating categories as dates
challenges.insightPrompt: Write one category comparison insight and a next action.
hints: Categories are discrete, not time.
Bar length supports comparison.
Use both scale and profitability.
challenges.explanation: Bars make categorical comparison easy; combining revenue, units and margin avoids optimizing on sales alone.

challenges.title: Spend vs Conversion Relationship
challenges.context: Marketing asks whether higher campaign spend tends to coincide with more conversions.
challenges.insightPrompt: Describe the relationship without claiming causation.
hints: Two numeric variables suggest a scatter plot.
Efficiency matters as well as volume.
Use association language.
challenges.explanation: Scatter plots show numeric relationships; efficiency KPIs help interpret whether extra spend is productive.

challenges.title: Retention Cohort View
challenges.context: Product wants to know whether newer signup cohorts retain better over months since signup.
challenges.insightPrompt: Write one insight comparing newer and older cohorts.
hints: Cohort analysis has two time dimensions.
Heatmaps expose retention decay patterns.
Always show cohort size.
challenges.explanation: Cohort heatmaps make retention decay comparable while cohort size guards against overreading tiny groups.

challenges.title: Conversion Funnel Dashboard
challenges.context: Growth wants to identify the stage with the largest conversion loss.
challenges.prompt: Choose the chart and KPI set.
chartOptions: Funnel or ordered stage bar chart
challenges.expectedChart: Funnel or ordered stage bar chart
hints: Stages have a defined order.
Show both counts and rates.
Focus action on the largest meaningful drop.
challenges.explanation: Funnel views preserve stage order and expose where users are lost.

challenges.title: Executive Operations Scorecard
challenges.context: Hospital operations leadership wants one page for demand, wait, throughput and capacity pressure.
challenges.prompt: Choose the chart style and KPI set.
chartOptions: Small KPI scorecards plus trend/exception charts
challenges.expectedChart: Small KPI scorecards plus trend/exception charts
challenges.insightPrompt: Write the headline executive message that should accompany the scorecard.
hints: Executives need a small decision set.
Mix level KPIs with trend/exception visuals.
Avoid decorative metrics.
challenges.explanation: Executive dashboards should emphasize a small causal/operational chain rather than maximize chart count.

challenges.title: Spot a Misleading Axis
challenges.context: A bar chart compares delinquency rates of 4.8% and 5.1% but the y-axis starts at 4.7%.
challenges.prompt: Choose the safer visual treatment and KPI set.
chartOptions: Bar or dot plot with a non-misleading scale and explicit labels
Keep the truncated axis because it makes the change easier to see
challenges.expectedChart: Bar or dot plot with a non-misleading scale and explicit labels
challenges.insightPrompt: Explain the real change and why the original chart could mislead.
hints: The absolute difference is 0.3 percentage points.
A truncated bar baseline exaggerates visual size.
Show denominator/count context too.
challenges.explanation: Chart scales should not visually exaggerate small differences; denominators and absolute counts add context.
